claims.text: Controlled interfacial layers based on defect-engineered carbon supports or graphene shells reduce atomic mobility in multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
Defect-engineered carbon supports provide enhanced anchoring sites that physically fix nanoparticles.
A conformal graphene shell physically fixes the nanoparticles and suppresses their atomic diffusion.
Reduced atomic mobility caused by the engineered interface mitigates phase segregation.
Engineered interfaces mitigate nanoparticle coalescence at high temperature.
Enhanced interfacial interactions reduce nanoparticle surface diffusion and atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility impedes the nucleation and growth of segregated phases.
Interfacial anchoring preserves the chemical homogeneity of solid-solution nanoparticles.
Interfacial anchoring prevents nanoparticle coarsening under high-temperature conditions.
Engineered-interface nanoparticles will undergo significantly less phase segregation, coalescence, and structural degradation than nanoparticles on untreated supports.
Nanoparticles on untreated carbon supports have higher atomic-diffusion rates that lead to phase segregation and coalescence at high temperature.
The stabilizing effect operates throughout catalytic service temperatures of 773–1173 K.
The stabilizing effect operates under thermoelectric conditions up to 1923 K.
The stabilizing effect persists when the nanoparticles contain low noble-metal contents.
The as-synthesized, unanchored near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles are metastable.
The proposed mechanism applies to multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles that begin with homogeneous elemental dispersions.
The magnitude of mobility and segregation suppression varies with the exact interfacial modification.
